pointers.sentence: The release notes give the reason for adding one: a policy tells the browser which scripts, styles and images a page may load, a defence against content injection such as cross-site scripting (`docs/releases/6.0.txt`).
Each is a dictionary from a directive to its sources, and each is empty by default, which writes no header (`django/conf/global_settings.py`).

`CSP`, in `django.utils.csp`, is a string enumeration of the two headers' names, of some of the specification's quoted keywords, such as `CSP.SELF`, and of one placeholder of Django's own, `CSP.NONCE`, which stands in a directive for the request's nonce (`django/utils/csp.py:CSP`).

`build_policy` puts the nonce in place of the placeholder only if something in the request read it, and otherwise drops it (`django/middleware/csp.py:ContentSecurityPolicyMiddleware`, `django/utils/csp.py:build_policy`).

`build_policy` puts the nonce in place of the placeholder only if something in the request read it, and otherwise drops it (`django/middleware/csp.py:ContentSecurityPolicyMiddleware`, `django/utils/csp.py:build_policy`).
The context processor `django.template.context_processors.csp` puts the nonce in a template's context as `"csp_nonce"` (`django/template/context_processors.py:csp`).

`csp_override` and `csp_report_only_override` give one view's response a policy that replaces the setting's whole, and an empty dictionary leaves that header off (`django/views/decorators/csp.py:_make_csp_decorator`).
A project has no policy until it asks for one: the settings module startproject writes lists neither the middleware nor the processor (`django/conf/project_template/project_name/settings.py-tpl`).

`{% csp_nonce_attr %}` writes `nonce="…"` from the context's `"csp_nonce"`, and given a `Media` renders it with that attribute on each `MediaAsset` in it; with no nonce in the context it writes none (`django/utils/csp.py:nonce_attr`) ([The built-in tags](../templates/tags.md)).

Django's own templates write it too since 6.1: the `<script>`, `<style>` and `<link>` elements of the admin's templates, the documentation generator's and the CSRF failure page carry the tag, and `csrf_failure`, which renders that page with an engine of its own, adds the processor's dictionary to its context (`django/views/csrf.py:csrf_failure`).
It is not a deployment check, so it runs on every check (`django/core/checks/security/base.py:check_csp_nonce_context_processor`) ([The security checks](../security/checks.md)).

`HttpResponseBase.set_signed_cookie` signs with the signer of `get_cookie_signer`, given a salt that `_cookie_signer_salt` makes from the cookie's name and the caller's salt (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponseBase.set_signed_cookie`).
Until 5.2.15 and 6.0.6 that salt was the name followed by the caller's salt, so that two pairs could make one string and a cookie be accepted where it had not been signed (`docs/releases/6.0.6.txt`).

At this commit the salt is `"django.http.cookies.v2:"`, the length of the caller's salt, a colon, that salt and the name; the comment says the length is there so that the pairs cannot collide (`django/core/signing.py:_cookie_signer_salt`).
`HttpRequest.get_signed_cookie` reads through `_unsign_cookie`, which checks the signature under the new salt (`django/core/signing.py:_unsign_cookie`).

In 5.2.15 and 6.0.6 it was on by default, so that cookies signed before the fix stayed good (`docs/ref/settings.txt`); since 6.1 its default is false, and the setting is deprecated, to go with the old salt in Django 2028, and warns when a project sets it ([What changed in settings, startup and the commands](startup-and-commands.md)).
The messages' `CookieStorage` passes a salt of its own to `get_cookie_signer` directly, and the fallback has no part in it (`django/contrib/messages/storage/cookie.py:CookieStorage.__init__`).

`salted_hmac` and `base64_hmac` given no algorithm use SHA-1, as before, and since 6.1 warn with `RemovedInDjango2028Warning`; in Django 2028 the default becomes SHA-256 (`django/utils/crypto.py:salted_hmac`, `django/core/signing.py:base64_hmac`).

`Signer.__init__` takes keyword arguments only: positional ones, deprecated in 4.2, were removed in 5.1, and `TimestampSigner` has the same `__init__` (`django/core/signing.py:Signer.__init__`).
It came in 4.1, when `CsrfViewMiddleware` stopped masking the secret in its cookie, to keep the cookie masked while a project's instances were upgraded (`docs/releases/4.1.txt`).

The cookie holds the secret itself, 32 characters (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._set_csrf_cookie`), and a cookie of 64, a masked secret, is still accepted and unmasked as it is read (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._get_secret`) ([The CSRF secret and its token](../security/csrf-token.md)).
